citations.narrative:
The facility failed to handle nonhuman primates in a manner that minimizes the risk of harm to the animals and the public
during a public exhibition. On July 8, 2026, Caesar, a seven-year-old black-handed spider monkey, injured a child while
the licensee was exhibiting the monkeys to a group of children. According to the licensee, Caesar was on a 15-foot leash
and eating applesauce off plates that the children were holding. Caesar was close to the children with no barriers between
them. The licensee says that a child touched Caesar's tail and Caesar reacted by scratching the child and breaking skin.
He saw the interaction as it was happening, but Caesar's reaction was too fast for him to retract the monkey with the
leash. While investigating the incident, inspectors learned that the child received medical attention from a medical
provider after the injury and required rabies post-exposure prophylaxis treatment several weeks later.
Failure to handle animals in a manner that minimizes risk can result in injury or be harmful to the health and well-being of
the animal or the public.
During public exhibition, any animal must be handled so there is minimal risk of harm to the animal and to the public, with
sufficient distance and/or barriers between the animals and the general public so as to assure the safety of animals and
the public.

The primary enclosure for the one rabbit was not kept reasonably free of excreta and cobwebs. Several areas of the wire
floor of the enclosure had rabbit feces measuring approximately five by give inches. Much of the mesh on the front and
sides of the enclosure were covered in cobwebs and hay. The licensee told inspectors that he could not remember the
last time the enclosure was cleaned.
Inadequate frequency of cleaning to remove excreta and other debris may lead to the spread of disease hazards, create
unpleasant odors, or attract pests.
Correct by keeping primary enclosures of rabbits reasonable free of excreta, hair, cobwebs, and other debris by periodic
cleaning.

Food used to feed non-human primates was not stored in a manner that protects the supplies from spoilage,
contamination, and vermin infestation. Inspectors observed the bag of primate biscuits currently being fed to two black-
handed spider monkeys on the floor and standing open. The food was in the original packaging and was the bag was
approximately 30% full. The licensee told inspectors that he usually kept primate food in a sealed container but had not
put this bag in a sealed container.
Improper food storage may reduce nutritional value and palatability and increase contamination and pests. Open food
items must be kept in leakproof, tightly sealed containers to prevent spoilage, contamination, and pest infestation.
Correct by storing food and bedding supplies off the floor and away from the walls. When not in actual use, keep open
food and bedding supplies in leakproof containers with tightly fitting lids to prevent spoilage, contamination, and vermin
infestation.

The primary enclosure housing two black-handed spider monkeys was not constructed nor maintained to protect the
nonhuman primates from injury. Three fluorescent light fixtures were hanging approximately 6-8 inches from the top of the
enclosure. The enclosure was topped with a section of chain-link fencing. The outlets, cords, and fixtures with fluorescent
tubes were all accessible to the animals inside the enclosure. Inspectors observed one of the monkeys reach through the
chain link and grasp a fluorescent tube.
Animal access to these items poses a risk for injury or death if the fluorescent tubes were to break or the animals were to
suffer electric shock.
Correct by constructing and maintaining primary enclosures for nonhuman primates so that they protect the non-human
primates from injury.
This inspection was an announced new site approval inspection.
This site is not ready for approval to conduct activity covered under your current Animal Welfare Act License.
Conducting regulated activities at a non-approved site is a violation of the Animal Welfare Act.
Please contact your inspector to schedule your next new site approval inspection.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of new site inspections must be received within 21
days of the original report issuance date (October 8, 2026).
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
Additional Inspectors:
